chapter_theme: Paalai: the road of separation, tigers, robbers, cairns and hero-stones, seen from home; the mother of an eloped girl (30), the friend before the man leaves (31, 36), the heroine's reproaches and fears (32-40), and omens of his return (41, 42).

29.reading: The speaker thinks of the hard wasteland whose paths are choked, where a speckled cock pecks at the striped maral, and of the mountain of the land of the one the gossip went out about, which now shows itself rising high on the right.
29.nuance: A hill seen rising on the right (வலன்) is the auspicious side, so the closing image may be an omen of the man's good journey or return, as in 41 and 42; but line 2 (அருஞ்சுரம்நரம்) and line 3 (அறிவிட்டு, கொடியக) are hard to construe, and the speaker and situation are our guess.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard wasteland the absent man crossed

30.reading: A mother whose daughter has gone off with a man wonders whether the girl sits pining, sighing that she cannot go on, or whether she walks behind that man like a killer elephant across the stony wasteland, the pebbles in her anklets ringing and her soft toes reddening.
30.nuance: The anklet is the unmarried girl's ornament (the silambu is removed at the wedding), so its ringing on the desert road says she has gone before her marriage rite. The addressee is no one present: the mother speaks to herself. மெல்விரல் may be fingers or toes; walking makes toes the likelier sense.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl's going with her lover through the wasteland

iraicchi.act: the bull elephant sleeps beside its mate in the thin shade of the burning forest rather than leaving her
iraicchi.sense: even the beasts of the road he means to cross keep to their mates in the heat, so the man should not leave her to cross it

31.reading: Under the dappled shade of the rough-barked omai a striped-trunked elephant sleeps with its mate, and when the man speaks of leaving through that fire-hazed forest the tears in the heroine's kohl-lined, red-streaked eyes will not stay.
31.nuance: The speaker is most likely the friend telling the man what his talk of going has already done: the tears come at the word, before any parting.

thinai_evidence.note: the man speaks of leaving through the burning forest

32.reading: The heroine says that the road is lined with lettered stones where archers with fine arrows harass the lovely way and fill the wasteland, and yet, fitting his labour that wins great things, his longing in love has become longing for hard-won wealth.
32.nuance: The lettered stones are hero-stones of men killed by the road's archers, so the danger and the motive are set side by side. ஏற்க, 'fitting', may be praise of his effort or a bitter concession; the poem leaves it open. Lines 1 and 2 are hard to divide (வாயில், அம்ஆ(று)), so the scene is read only in outline.

thinai_evidence.note: the road of hero-stones the man takes for wealth

33.reading: The heroine asks whether the man, whose heart without kindly regard for his soft girl climbs after wealth and will not stay, does not see on the road the men who live by ploughing with the bow, rushing out to harass travellers among the stone-ringed cairns.
33.nuance: The cairns are the stone heaps over travellers the robbers killed, so 'do they not see?' means: he can see the death on the road and still goes, but cannot see her.

thinai_evidence.note: the man leaves for wealth through the robbers' road

comparisons.tenor: the robbers who live off travellers as farmers live off the field

34.reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the man will cross the waterless hard road where herds of wild cattle roam, and whether her heart, throwing off shame, will go along with her life and contrive that she see him.
34.nuance: உயிரோடு உடன்சென்று: the heart will leave with her life, so following him and dying are the same act; shame is the only thing that keeps her body at home.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is to cross the waterless road

35.reading: The heroine asks whether the man with a heart without moisture does not know the waterless hard road, where the sharp-clawed bear's dark kin settle in an abandoned house overgrown with gourd vine and sleep.
35.nuance: If இருங்கினை stands for இருங்கிளை (the dark kin), the bears that sleep together in a deserted house are set against a man who leaves his own house: a near miss for iraicchi, kept as scene because the word is in doubt. The 'moistureless heart' answers the waterless road.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's journey over the waterless road

36.reading: The friend asks whether the man without sense will drive his chariot away through the forest, where squirrels squeal in the cane of the scrub and the village cock fights the quail round the garden plots, rather than ending the gossip the town has raised.
36.nuance: ஒழித்து can mean that he goes leaving the gossip behind for her to bear, or that he should end it by marrying; either way the journey is set against marriage. The scrub with its village, cock and quail is a mullai woodland on the paalai road. The fighting cock and quail may hint at the town's quarrel, but one match of mood is not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: the man leaves while the town gossips about the secret love

37.reading: The heroine asks whether the man will cross the tall-hilled road, where a creature that lost its mate to the leaping tiger crowds in fear at the sun-baked rock, the wasteland where the beast of prey watches for its kill.
37.nuance: துணையிழந்து அஞ்சி, a beast that has lost its mate and fears, is the fate she fears for herself, but the creature only suffers and does nothing a lover does, so it carries a mood, not an iraicchi. Line 2 (கடவு தெவுட்டு) is obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's crossing of the tiger's road

38.reading: The heroine asks whether he has crossed the forest of cairns and fallen blossom where the strong striped tiger, skilled at the kill, roars, he of a hero's strength who went far to finish his labour and does not understand what is good.
38.nuance: The praise is barbed: மீளி, the hero's might, and ஆள்வினை, manly labour, are the virtues that make him blind to the good at home. Line 1 (நல்வய மரக்குழுமும்) is probably a misdivision of a line about the tiger's roar.

thinai_evidence.note: he crossed the forest for his labour

39.reading: The heroine asks her own life whether it will live on, thinking of the grace of the man who went off in unreflecting desire for wealth on the road where a gape-mouthed tiger, having missed its elephant, watches the entrance of the common hall of a ruined village, or whether it will not.
39.nuance: The addressee is her own life (உயிர்), set apart from her as the heart is in other poems. The tiger that failed with an elephant and now waits at a ruined village for weaker prey makes the road dangerous to the man; the 'grace' she must live on is the very thing his going denies.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone for wealth across the ruined road

iraicchi.act: the wildcat goes out on the dangerous ground to watch for prey to feed its young
iraicchi.sense: the man too has gone out on the robbers' road to win what his household needs, so his going is provision as well as desertion

40.reading: The heroine says that the road her lover's heart set out on is, people say, a wasteland where robbers roam and where, in the plots ringed by tangled thorny bamboo, the spotted wildcat watches for prey for its kitten.
40.nuance: She has only heard of the road (என்பர், 'they say'); it is his heart, not his body, she follows along it.

41.reading: As the owl hoots from the old tree of the village common, bright sneezes come one after another, so the man who went over the hills and past the hill forts seems to be thinking of her in secret.
41.nuance: A sneeze was taken as a sign that someone far away is thinking of you; repeated sneezes mean steady thought. கள்ளிய தன்மையர், 'of a stealing nature', suggests he thinks of her secretly or is stealing back unannounced; the owl's cry is a second omen whose sense the poem does not spell out.

thinai_evidence.note: the heroine waits for the man who crossed the hills

42.reading: Her flower-like left eye throbs, her dreams have turned good, her swollen soft shoulders grow lovely again as she thinks of the man who crossed the high hills, and the lizard chirps at the favourable side.
42.nuance: Four omens are heaped up: the throbbing left eye (good for a woman), dreams that come right, the body's own return to beauty, and the lizard's chirp from the proper quarter. The body recovers before the man arrives. பிணைதீர and மெள்தோள் (for மென்தோள்) are uncertain in the text.

thinai_evidence.note: the heroine waits for the man who crossed the hills

links.note: Both mothers lament a daughter gone with a man through the bowmen's wasteland; Akananuru 35 prays to the god that the stranger may adorn her and lull her on his chest, while Ainthinai Ezhupathu 30 can only wonder whether the girl pines or walks on behind him with reddened feet.
links.teaches: Together they give the mother's lament two stages, first not knowing whether the girl regrets her going and then accepting it and praying for the man's care, so the venba catches the moment the Akananuru poem has already passed.

links.note: In Akananuru 91 the elephant that shrinks with its hungry mate in drought lets the friend reassure the heroine after the man has gone; in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 31 the elephant sleeping with its mate in the burning forest comes when the man only speaks of going, and her tears answer it.
links.teaches: The same iraicchi of the elephant pair keeping together in the heat serves to comfort after the parting and to dissuade before it, which shows the image carries the lovers' bond itself and the speaker turns it to whatever the moment needs.

links.note: Akananuru 53: past the lettered hero-stone of men felled by the archers' fine arrows, the heroine says his love is for wealth more than for her (பொருளே காதலர் காதல்). Ainthinai Ezhupathu 32 keeps the lettered stones, the archers' fine arrows and the claim that his love's longing has become hard-won wealth.
links.teaches: The venba compresses Akananuru 53's scene and accusation into four lines but drops the friend's defence that he goes from a giving heart, putting his 'fitting labour' in its place, so the later poem shows which part of the older argument had become formula and which part it chose to change.

links.note: Akananuru 35's road is held by bowmen of வில் ஏர் வாழ்க்கை, 'the life whose plough is the bow', and their cairns; Ainthinai Ezhupathu 33's road by வில்லுழுது உண்பார், 'those who eat by ploughing with the bow', among the cairns.
links.teaches: Held together they show the bow-as-plough figure for the wasteland robbers passing intact from the Sangam anthology into the later venba, while its use shifts from a mother's fear for a daughter on the road to a wife's reproach that the man can see the road's dangers but not her.

links.note: In Kural 1247 the woman in separation tells her heart to give up either desire or shame, since she cannot bear both; in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 34 she foresees her heart throwing off shame and going with her life after him.
links.teaches: The couplet poses the choice between desire and shame as a demand on the heart, and the venba shows the heart's answer and its cost, since choosing desire there means the life leaving the body with it.

links.note: In Akananuru 297 the man on his way for wealth sees a wildcat's fluffy kitten following its mother like stars round the moon; in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 40 the heroine hears that on his road the spotted wildcat watches for prey for its kitten.
links.teaches: Each lover sees the wildcat with its young on the wealth road from his or her own side, the man as the household he leaves behind and the woman as the provision he goes to win, so the creature gathers both halves of the paalai argument about leaving for wealth.

links.note: Kural 1203: a sneeze that seems to come and then dies away makes her think he seems about to think of her and does not. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 41: sneezes come one after another, so he is thinking of her. On the plain reading the same sign gives opposite verdicts.
links.teaches: Both women read the sneeze by the same folk belief, but the Kural uses its failure for a wry doubt while the venba piles it up as proof, which shows the belief was firm enough to support either despair or hope depending on what the body did.

links.note: In Akananuru 289 the man on his journey imagines her praying 'speak good' each time the lizard chirps; in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 42 the lizard chirps at the favourable side, together with a throbbing eye and good dreams.
links.teaches: The man's imagined picture of her waiting on the lizard and her own report that the lizard has spoken well are the two ends of one practice, which shows that the omen was a shared language the separated lovers each expected the other to be reading.

new_concepts.gloss: an omen read from the body or from creatures (sneezing, a throbbing eye, a lizard's chirp, an owl's cry) as a sign of the absent lover's thought or return
new_concepts.label_source: the Tholkappiyam's term for omens; the verses show the signs (தும்மல், பல்லி படும்)

source_issues: 29 line 2: அருஞ்சுரம்நரம் is not a word; perhaps அருஞ்சுரம் நாம் ('we, thinking of the hard road'). Lines 2-3 (அறிவிட்(டு), கொடியக) are hard to construe.
35 line 2: இருங்கினை is probably இருங்கிளை ('dark kin').
37 line 2: கடவு தெவுட்டு is obscure and may be corrupt.
38 line 1: நல்வய மரக்குழுமும் is probably a misdivision (நல்வயமாக் குழுமும், 'the strong beast roars').
39 line 3: அருள்நினைந் lacks its final syllable (அருள்நினைந்து).
41 line 2: குன்றனம் may stand for குன்றம்.
42 line 3: மெள்தோள் is a misprint for மென்தோள்; பிணைதீர is uncertain.
